title: Mysterious Lake Country find may be sturgeon bone, experts say
excerpt: A mysterious object pulled from the bottom of a Lake Country beach has some experts scratching their heads
content:
Lake find may be sturgeon

Photo: Clayton Brown

A Lake Country family's mysterious beach find near 50th Parallel Winery is a stumper

UPDATE 1:30 p.m

Experts from the Royal B.C. Museum have offered a preliminary theory on the mysterious object pulled from the bottom of Coral Beach near Lake Country's 50th Parallel Winery last week, and Ogopogo may be off the hook.

Dr. Bruce Archibald, curator of paleontology collections at the Beaty Biodiversity Museum at UBC, says his working theory is a sturgeon scute, a bony plate found on the fish's skin.

And one of the vertebrate zoologists at the Royal B.C. Museum has seconded that opinion.

"My knee-jerk response is sturgeon bone. The edges are weathered, so not the exact shape it once had, but it looks like it has lateral line canal grooves and I can't think of any other freshwater fish in our waterways with scutes or bones with this texture," the zoologist said.

The experts didn't rule out other possibilities, however, suggesting the object could also be something less local, such as a bone from a gar pike skull or a shell from a softshell turtle, species not native to the Okanagan that could have ended up in the lake another way.

Clayton Brown and his daughter Chloe found the object while diving off a dock at Coral Beach, roughly eight feet down in soft, sandy bottom.

There have been reports of sturgeon in Okanagan Lake going back a century, although those sightings have never been verified. What appears to be a sturgeon skull was found in the lake in 2022.

ORIGINAL 4:00 a.m.

A mysterious object pulled from the bottom of a Lake Country beach has some experts scratching their heads.

Clayton Brown tells Castanet he was enjoying a day at the beach with his family, swimming and doing some underwater exploring at Coral Beach, a small stretch of shoreline just below 50th Parallel Winery last Wednesday.

His daughter, Chloe, jumped off the dock and started scanning the lake bottom for treasure when she spotted something white and unusual.

"Sometimes she finds tiny little shells and stuff like that... And then she just found this really unique piece, and we're just like, 'What the heck is this?' And we just have absolutely no idea. It's quite different and interesting from anything we've ever seen there," says Brown.

Chloe made the discovery in about eight feet of water just off the dock, in the soft, sandy bottom. Brown says he went back the next day and combed the same spot by hand, hoping to turn up a matching piece. But he came up empty.

Brown says he didn't know where to start to try and figure out what he was looking at, so he sent it to Castanet.

"I don't know if there are geologists in town, or if we should take it to the museum," he said.

Stumped, Brown reached out to a friend in Calgary whose wife works as a geologist. She told him it looked like a fossil, but couldn't say of what.

Castanet shared the photo with Dr. Bruce Archibald, curator of paleontology collections at the Beaty Biodiversity Museum at UBC and the Royal B.C. Museum.

"That sure looks interesting. I'm not familiar with this," Archibald said.

The object itself is hard to pin down. Brown said the underside has the texture of sandpaper, while the top is covered in a different pattern altogether, something he compares to bone or cartilage, split down the middle. His wife thought it resembled an arrowhead, depending on the angle it is viewed.

Archibald, whose specialty is fossil insects rather than vertebrates, said his first guess was that it could be part of a fish, but he's passing the photos along to a colleague who studies vertebrate fossils for their opinion.

Museum staff asked for more photos that show the size of the object.

For now, the origin of the object remains an open question, although Brown's original email subject heading was titled: 'Ogopogo's tooth?'

Castanet will update this story as more information becomes available.

Photo: Clayton Brown

A Lake Country family's mysterious beach find near 50th Parallel Winery has stumped a Calgary geologist and a UBC paleontologist, with one tipster jokingly suggesting it could be Ogopogo's tooth.
